notes:
I've written notes on 1 Peter 3 below, but the research is incomplete: the search tool hit its usage limit partway through. Each note comes only from a page I actually read, or from the page extract the search tool returned, with its URL. Read these gaps first:

- **Verses 19–22 from Enduring Word:** the page cut off partway through verse 18, so I have nothing from it on 19–22.
- **Gill, Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary on verses 1–17:** I never got to these, so the "traditional reading" for 1–17 rests mainly on Enduring Word (which quotes Grudem, Spurgeon, Morgan and others) plus Matthew Henry on 14–17.
- **Missing views:** I found nothing from Methodist or Wesleyan teachers, Pentecostal teachers, the Orthodox Church (oca.org), modern scholarship (netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org), or popular movements like prosperity or hyper-grace teaching. They are left out, not looked at and found to have no view.
- **Verses 8–12 and 22** have only thin notes.

---

**v. 1:** Guzik says submission is God's order for the home, not a reward the husband earns. The Greek word was used of soldiers placed under their officers. He quotes Grudem that this doesn't make wives lesser persons. It applies to a wife's *own* husband, not to men in general, and it ends where obeying would mean sinning (Acts 4:19–20). The background was a new Christian wife asking whether to leave her unbelieving husband or act superior to him. "Do not obey the word" means active disobedience, not just unbelief. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-3/

**v. 2:** Guzik says a wife wins her husband through pure conduct and the fear of God, not persuasive lectures. Pressing him with her own words can get in the way of God's work. He quotes Grudem that a husband senses inwardly that this behaviour is right, and so concludes the gospel is true. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-3/

**v. 3:** Guzik says Peter isn't banning hairstyles or jewellery, any more than clothes ("fine" isn't in the Greek). He's saying these shouldn't be where a woman's beauty comes from. Citing Barclay, Guzik says women then often dyed their hair and wore wigs. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-3/

**v. 4:** Guzik says inner beauty is "incorruptible": it doesn't fade with age but grows. A gentle and quiet spirit isn't prized by our culture, but it is precious to God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-3/

**v. 5:** Guzik says this is not a new standard but what holy women always practised. Behind both submission and plain dress is trust in God rather than in one's own control or looks. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-3/

**v. 6:** Guzik says Sarah obeyed Abraham even when he was wrong (Genesis 12:10–20), and honoured him by calling him "lord." True submission involves both obedience and honour. "Do good and not fear" means it is an active, trusting acceptance of God's will, not sulking surrender. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-3/

**v. 7:** Guzik makes these points: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-3/
- The husband must truly live with his wife and put his understanding of her into practice.
- The word for "wife" here is rare and means "the feminine one."
- In a Roman world where husbands held almost all the rights, giving husbands duties toward their wives was radical.
- "Weaker" means physically weaker, not spiritually.
- "Joint heirs" means wives are spiritually equal (Grudem).
- "Your prayers" means the husband's own prayers. Spurgeon is quoted that anything in family life that hinders prayer must be changed.

**v. 8:** Guzik says "one mind" means the mind of Christ, learned from Scripture. That is unity, not sameness, like a choir singing in harmony. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-3/

**v. 9:** Guzik says the real test of love comes when we are wronged. Only Christ's love breaks the cycle of revenge. We bless partly for our own sake, because blessing others leads to inheriting a blessing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-3/

**vv. 10–12:** These verses quote Psalm 34. Guzik says evil is usually rewarded at once and good later, but the rewards of good are better and surer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-3/

**v. 13:** Guzik says "followers" literally means "be zealous" (citing Hart). He quotes F. B. Meyer that never being hated by the world is a dangerous place for a Christian to be. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-3/

**v. 14:** Guzik says God especially cares for those who suffer unjustly, and links this to Matthew 10:28. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-3/

**v. 15:**
- Guzik notes that some manuscripts read "sanctify Christ as Lord." He quotes G. Campbell Morgan: one Lord at the centre of life, with no rivals such as self or other people's opinions. Being ready to answer requires knowing the Bible, and Peter himself did this in Acts 2–5 by the Spirit's power. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-3/
- Matthew Henry says we honour God before others when our conduct leads them to glorify Him. Our faith should be defended with meekness, in the fear of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_peter/3-19.htm

**v. 16:** Guzik says good conduct under ill-treatment proves accusers wrong and shames them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-3/ Henry says a good conscience is one that does its job well. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_peter/3-19.htm

**v. 17:** Guzik says some Christians suffer for being obnoxious and call it persecution. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-3/ Henry says a person who has both sin and suffering is in a sad state. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_peter/3-19.htm

**v. 18:**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says Christ's one sacrifice is final, and our own suffering can't pay for sin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-3/ Henry says Christ died in His human nature and was raised by the Holy Spirit, to bring us to God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_peter/3-19.htm
- **Debate over "made alive in the Spirit / in spirit":**
  - A Gospel Coalition article says it means the Holy Spirit (comparing Romans 8). https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/does-1-peter-teach-jesus-preached-hell/
  - Barnes says it means Christ's divine nature. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_peter/3-19.htm
  - Ellicott rejects "by the Spirit" and reads "in spirit," meaning Christ as a spirit without His body. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_peter/3-19.htm

**v. 19 (the most debated verse):**
- **View 1, Christ preached through Noah:** Christ, by His Spirit, preached through Noah to people who are now spirits in prison.
  - A Gospel Coalition article argues this is the best reading. It points to 2 Peter 2:5, where Noah is a "herald of righteousness." https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/does-1-peter-teach-jesus-preached-hell/
  - Benson, Barnes and Matthew Henry hold this view. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_peter/3-19.htm
  - Clarke and Coffman hold it too. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-peter/3-19.html
  - A Ligonier devotional (Reformed) takes it as "likely" and denies that Christ's spirit went to hell. It cites "today in Paradise" to the thief and says the atoning work was finished on the cross. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/christs-descent-into-hell
  - Grudem, quoted at Precept Austin, asks why Christ would preach only to Noah's generation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_peter_318-22
  - Ellicott says this view was held by Pearson, Leighton, Aquinas and Beza, but thinks it makes the passage pointless. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_peter/3-19.htm
- **View 2, Christ went to the dead between His death and resurrection:**
  - Ellicott says this was the view of almost all the Church Fathers, Calvin, Luther (in the end), Bellarmine, Bengel and most scholars of his day, and he holds it himself. He thinks Christ brought some kind of good news (linking 1 Peter 4:6), and rejects the idea of announcing their damnation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_peter/3-19.htm
- **View 3, a victory announcement to fallen angels:**
  - The Ryrie Study Bible, cited at Precept Austin, links this to 2 Peter 2:4–5 and the "sons of God" of Genesis 6. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_peter_318-22
  - A Bible Hub Q&A page favours this view, citing 2 Peter 2:4–5, Jude 6–7 and Colossians 2:15. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_1_Peter_3_19_preached_to_spirits.htm
  - The Gospel Coalition article doubts it, because verse 20 seems to describe humans. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/does-1-peter-teach-jesus-preached-hell/
- **Lutheran view:** Christ went to hell to announce His triumph over death and the devil, and Lutherans take this verse as the clearest teaching of that. https://witness.lcms.org/2010/did-jesus-really-visit-hell-if-yes-why-2-2010/ An LCMS study of Formula of Concord Article IX reads the verse as a victory proclamation. It contrasts Calvin, who took the creed's "descended into hell" as Christ's inner suffering. https://resources.lcms.org/reading-study/formula-of-concord-study-article-ix/ A 1517 sermon resource treats the passage as "our Lord's harrowing of Hell." https://www.1517.org/articles/epistle-1-peter-313-22-easter-6-series-a-2026
- **Reformed (R. C. Sproul):** Sproul says the Bible is "less than clear." The "spirits in prison" could be lost people in this world, and Peter doesn't say where the prison is. https://www.ligonier.org/learn/qas/what-does-apostles-creed-mean-when-it-says-jesus-d
- **Catholic view:** Following the Catechism (632–633), Christ's soul went to the realm of the dead "as Savior." He preached the good news to the righteous waiting in "Abraham's bosom" and freed them. He did not free the damned. https://www.catholic.com/qa/what-he-descended-into-hell-means Aquinas is quoted on Christ freeing the holy fathers. https://www.catholic.com/qa/the-afterlife-of-the-old-testament-just-souls
- **Explainer:** Got Questions explains the "harrowing of hell" idea, which also draws on Ephesians 4:9. https://www.gotquestions.org/harrowing-of-hell.html
- **Second chance after death:** The Gospel Coalition article mentions this view and rejects it, citing Hebrews 9:27. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/does-1-peter-teach-jesus-preached-hell/

**v. 20:**
- Benson says the 120 years of Genesis 6:3 were God's patience waiting for repentance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_peter/3-19.htm
- Henry says the disobedient are now in hell, with no redemption. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_peter/3-19.htm
- Greever (Desiring God) presents Noah as a righteous sufferer whom God later vindicated. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/baptism-now-saves-you

**v. 21 (traditions differ):**
- **Baptist:**
  - Joshua Greever (Desiring God) says baptism is not regenerating in itself; it expresses faith. The flood was the occasion of salvation, and the ark was the means. Christ is the "ark," and immersion pictures passing through judgment. "Appeal" (a request for a clean conscience) is a better translation than "pledge." https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/baptism-now-saves-you
  - John Piper says Peter immediately qualifies his words to stop them being read as baptismal regeneration. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/what-is-baptism-and-does-it-save
- **Reformed:** A Ligonier devotional says the ceremony doesn't save automatically; trust in Christ, shown in the appeal for forgiveness, saves. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/baptism-and-salvation
- **Lutheran:**
  - A 1517 article says salvation is given as a pure gift in, with and through baptism. You can appeal to God that by your baptism you are clean. https://www.1517.org/articles/baptism-now-saves-but-who-and-when
  - Another 1517 resource calls "baptism now saves" God acting through Word and water. It says the verse is richer than a "gotcha" against those who reject sacraments. https://www.1517.org/articles/epistle-1-peter-313-22-easter-6-series-a-2026
- **Catholic (described by a Baptist critic, not by a Catholic site):** Greever says the Catholic view is that baptism washes away sin, gives new life, and brings a person into the church, effecting what it signifies (Catechism §1234; Aquinas). https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/baptism-now-saves-you
- **General note:** Bible Hub's study notes call baptism an outward expression of inward faith and link it to Acts 2:38. https://biblehub.com/study/1_peter/3-21.htm
- **Translation:** Versions render the key phrase as "pledge," "appeal," "answer" and "interrogation." https://biblehub.com/1_peter/3-21.htm

**v. 22:** Guzik's opening summary says Christ, though He suffered for doing good, triumphed in the end and sits at God's right hand. That shows suffering for good ends in blessing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-3/ The Bible Hub Q&A page counts Christ's exaltation over all powers as the third proof of His triumph. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_1_Peter_3_19_preached_to_spirits.htm
